topic: Effect of free-shipping thresholds on conversion rate, average order value and returns in online retail

key_points.point: Shipping costs are a major conversion barrier: a Baymard survey (Feb 2024, 1,012 US adults) found 48% abandoned a cart because extra costs such as shipping, tax or fees were too high.

Lewis, Singh and Fay (Marketing Science 2006): consumers are very sensitive to shipping charges; fees affect both purchase incidence and basket size, and threshold free shipping generates extra sales but can be unprofitable.

Hirche et al. (2021): at a European retailer (26.2M orders) moving to a EUR 2.95 fee with EUR 20 free threshold raised sales (about +45%) and orders (+44%) where fees fell; conversion not measured directly.

Same study: threshold policy had no significant effect on order value, while return probability rose slightly (e.g. 52.30% to 54.56% in the fee-decrease group); filler items added to reach the threshold were returned less.

Shehu et al. (J Marketing Research, 2020): free shipping raised purchase incidence (.404 vs .397) and return share (.337 vs .333) in a field experiment, mainly via riskier products; simulation: volume +11% but profit -0.7%.

Simulation (Becerril-Arreola, Leng, Parlar, EJOR 2013): a USD 75 threshold raised mean order size (63.13 vs 58.61 baseline) but conversion was 19.40% versus 21.65% for free shipping on all orders (baseline 18.37%).

Evidence on average order value is mixed: observational natural experiment found no significant effect, while simulations and vendor A/B tests report increases; effect depends on how far the threshold sits above typical baskets.
Profitability depends on margin and return-handling cost: with 42.5% gross margin a threshold beat fixed fees for return costs up to EUR 12 per return; free shipping can lift volume yet cut profit.

An Intelligems vendor A/B test (one sports brand) raising a USD 100 threshold to USD 500 reported AOV about +6% and revenue per visitor about +12%; conversion effect is stated inconsistently and profit not reported.
Model results suggest the optimal threshold is high and rises with shipping cost relative to inventory costs (about USD 156 in the base simulation), so no universal threshold exists.
Generalizability caveat: the most rigorous studies come from single European retailers or simulations, and vendor case studies carry commercial interest; category and customer segment matter.
